stories.description: Anthropic thinks “closing the loop” is the best path to AI triumph—and a recipe for “existential” threats to humanity.

passages.author: Kaku
passages.passage: Douglas Lenat has devoted a lifetime to conquering the mysteries of common sense. He feels that the problem is that artificial intelligence (AT) researchers have tiptoed around the periphery of the real problem. What is needed, he says, is nothing less than an “AI Manhattan Project,” a full frontal assault on common sense.
passages.title: Visions
passages.why: Lenat's call for a massive, coordinated AI push anticipates today's race toward transformative AI capability—while quietly reframing the urgency: even well-intentioned "Manhattan Projects" can produce existential dangers alongside breakthroughs.

passages.author: Weiner
passages.passage: The introduction of the new devices and the dates at which they are to be expected are, of course, largely economic matters, on which I am not an expert. Short of any violent political changes or another great war, I should give a rough estimate that it will take the new tools ten to twenty years to come into their own. A war would change all this overnight.
passages.title: Human Use...Beings
passages.why: Wiener's warning that war could overnight accelerate technologies otherwise decades away reframes today's AI race as exactly the kind of crisis-driven pressure that bypasses the gradual, careful adoption he considered safer.

cluster.summary: This cluster orbits an irreducible paradox: the simultaneous collapse and persistence of heroic self-conception in modernity. Beginning with the classical hero's journey—Odysseus's arduous return to meaning and order—these works trace how the very structures that once sustained heroic action (narrative coherence, moral clarity, purposeful struggle) have become sources of paralysis and despair.

stories.description: It feels like everyone we know is talking about the new documentary You Can See Everything. It tracks the effort of comedian and documentarian Nathan Fielder to suss out how deceptive Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced founder of the company Theranos, is. And after watching the film, we all left the theater wondering -- what could we see? How possible is it to ever really spot someone lying? So we of course called up an expert in deception and counter-deception research, Maria Hartwig, a professor of psychology at CUNY, the City University of New York. For more on sussing out a liar, check out our episode about what's wrong with the polygraph. Interested in more deep dives on the science behind pop culture blockbusters? passages.author: Enns
passages.passage: The are no simple rules for how to conduct yourself. Hemingway's quip that “I only know that moral is what you feel good before and immoral is what you feel bad after” ' can take you only so far. One good principle to follow as a professional is what W call the “light-of-day” test.
passages.title: Clients for Life
passages.why: The "light-of-day" test—asking whether you'd be comfortable if your actions were exposed—reframes Holmes's deception as ultimately self-defeating, since full transparency, exactly what Fielder pursues, becomes the unavoidable moral reckoning.

passages.author: Ackerman
passages.passage: The world is a construct the brain builds based on the sensory information it’s given, and the information is only a small part of all that’s available. We can modify our senses through bat detectors, binoculars, telescopes, and microscopes, broadening that sensory horizon, and there are instruments that allow us to become a kind of sensory predator that natural selection never meant us to be.
passages.title: A History of the Senses
passages.why: The passage reframes the documentary's lie-detection quest as a fundamentally limited endeavor, since human senses only capture a fraction of available reality and spotting deception may require tools beyond our natural perceptual reach.

stories.description: Every day, Wikipedia biographies of living people are flagged for deletion because the subjects are not “notable” enough. How do these poor souls take the news?

passages.author: Mailer
passages.passage: Part of the art of being a novelist is to play that delicate game of obtaining experience without falsifying it by the act of observation. Generally speaking, it’s easier to take in such knowledge when you are part of an event that is much larger than yourself —like the fall of the Twin Towers.
passages.title: The Spooky Art
passages.why: Mailer's warning that observation falsifies experience reframes the Wikipedia deletion story as a case where being formally "noted" by others can distort or even erase a person's authentic significance.

passages.author: Orland
passages.passage: Try, if you can, to reoccupy your own aesthetic space of a few years back, or even a few months. There is no way. You can only plunge ahead, even when that carries with it the bittersweet realization that you have already done your very best work.
passages.title: Art and Fear
passages.why: The fear of irrelevance that haunts artists—that your best work may already be behind you—mirrors the quiet devastation of learning the world has decided you no longer merit remembering.

stories.title: The Tragedy of Having a Wikipedia Page—and Then Losing It
stories.why: Mailer's warning that observation falsifies experience reframes the Wikipedia deletion story as a case where being formally "noted" by others can distort or even erase a person's authentic significance.
